title: Australia, Primary and Secondary
subject: other-countries
year_note: Australian primary and secondary content, roughly ages 7 to 14. The NZ year band is a rough equivalent by age, not a curriculum match.

questions.prompt: What is the capital city of Australia?
questions.explanation: Canberra, not Sydney or Melbourne, was purpose built to be Australia's capital city.

questions.prompt: Which Australian city is famous for its Opera House and Harbour Bridge?
questions.explanation: Sydney's Opera House and Harbour Bridge are two of Australia's most recognisable landmarks.

questions.prompt: What is the capital city of Victoria?
questions.explanation: Melbourne, on the south east coast, is the capital of Victoria.

questions.prompt: What is the capital city of Queensland?
questions.explanation: Brisbane, on the Brisbane River, is the capital of Queensland.

questions.prompt: What is the capital city of Western Australia?
questions.explanation: Perth, on Australia's west coast, is the capital of Western Australia.

questions.prompt: What is the capital city of South Australia?
questions.explanation: Adelaide is the capital of South Australia, set between hills and the coast.

questions.prompt: What is the capital city of Tasmania, an island state south of the mainland?
questions.explanation: Hobart, on the Derwent River, is the capital of Tasmania.

questions.prompt: What is the capital city of the Northern Territory?
questions.explanation: Darwin, on Australia's tropical north coast, is the capital of the Northern Territory.

questions.prompt: The world's largest coral reef system lies off the coast of which Australian state?
questions.explanation: The Great Barrier Reef stretches along the Queensland coast and is the largest coral reef system in the world.

questions.prompt: Which two rivers make up Australia's largest river system, flowing through several south eastern states?
questions.explanation: The Murray-Darling river system drains a huge area of south eastern Australia and is vital for farming.

questions.prompt: Much of central Australia is covered by dry, sparsely populated land often called what?
questions.explanation: The outback is the vast, dry interior of Australia, home to deserts, red earth and small remote towns.

questions.prompt: Which large desert covers part of central Australia, near the border of South Australia, Queensland and the Northern Territory?
questions.explanation: The Simpson Desert is one of several deserts covering much of central Australia, known for its long red sand dunes.

questions.prompt: Which territory, though small, is entirely surrounded by New South Wales?
questions.explanation: The Australian Capital Territory, home to Canberra, is a small territory carved out of, and surrounded by, New South Wales.

questions.prompt: Which mountain range runs along Australia's east coast, from Queensland down through New South Wales to Victoria?
questions.explanation: The Great Dividing Range runs the length of Australia's eastern side and is the country's most extensive mountain range.

questions.prompt: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples are recognised as having lived in Australia for how long, making theirs the oldest continuous culture in the world?
questions.explanation: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples have lived on this land for at least 65,000 years, making theirs the oldest continuous culture on Earth.

questions.prompt: In 1788, a fleet of British ships arrived at what is now Sydney to set up a colony. What was this fleet called?
questions.explanation: The First Fleet, carrying convicts and officials from Britain, arrived in 1788 and founded the colony that became Sydney.

questions.prompt: Which day is a national day of remembrance in Australia, honouring those who served in war, especially at Gallipoli?
questions.explanation: Anzac Day, on 25 April, remembers Australian and New Zealand soldiers, first marking the landing at Gallipoli in 1915.

questions.prompt: In which year did six separate British colonies join together to form the single nation of Australia?
questions.explanation: Australia became a single federated nation on 1 January 1901, when the six colonies agreed to join together.

questions.prompt: What is the word for the six colonies joining together in 1901 to form one country?
questions.explanation: Federation is the name for the process by which Australia's separate colonies united under one national government in 1901.

questions.prompt: ANZAC is short for which group of soldiers who landed at Gallipoli in 1915?
choices: Australian and New Zealand Army Corps
questions.explanation: ANZAC stands for the Australian and New Zealand Army Corps, whose soldiers fought together at Gallipoli in 1915.

questions.prompt: The First Fleet in 1788 carried many people to Australia who had been sentenced to what?
questions.explanation: Many people on the First Fleet were convicts transported from Britain, sent to serve their sentences in the new colony.

questions.prompt: The Eureka Stockade of 1854 was a rebellion by workers in which industry, angry about licence fees?
questions.explanation: The Eureka Stockade saw gold miners in Victoria rebel against the government over unfair licence fees and a lack of political rights.

questions.prompt: In which Australian colony did the Eureka Stockade rebellion of 1854 take place?
questions.explanation: The Eureka Stockade happened near Ballarat, in the colony of Victoria, during the gold rush years.

questions.prompt: The Gallipoli campaign of 1915, where Anzac troops landed, took place during which war?
questions.explanation: The Gallipoli campaign was part of the First World War, as Allied forces tried and failed to take control of the Gallipoli peninsula.

questions.prompt: Before Federation in 1901, Australia was made up of how many separate British colonies?
questions.explanation: New South Wales, Victoria, Queensland, South Australia, Western Australia and Tasmania were six separate colonies before Federation.

questions.prompt: Gallipoli is a peninsula located in which present day country?
questions.explanation: Gallipoli is a peninsula in what is now Turkey, on the western side of the Dardanelles strait.

questions.prompt: Captain James Cook charted Australia's east coast in 1770, sailing on behalf of which country?
questions.explanation: James Cook charted the eastern coast of Australia in 1770 while sailing on behalf of Great Britain, ahead of the First Fleet's arrival in 1788.

questions.prompt: Which day, held on 26 January, marks the anniversary of the First Fleet's arrival and is a public holiday, though it is seen very differently by many Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people?
questions.explanation: Australia Day falls on 26 January, the anniversary of the First Fleet's 1788 arrival, and its meaning is understood very differently across the community.

questions.prompt: The Eureka Stockade is sometimes described by historians as an early step toward what, because of its calls for the vote and fairer representation?
choices: Self government for all colonies immediately
questions.explanation: Although the rebellion was crushed, many of the miners' demands for fairer representation were later adopted, and Eureka is often remembered as an early moment in Australian democracy.

questions.prompt: Aboriginal stone fish traps found at Brewarrina in New South Wales are considered among the world's oldest surviving examples of what?
questions.explanation: The stone fish traps at Brewarrina are thought to be among the oldest surviving human made structures anywhere in the world.

questions.prompt: Which large Australian animal hops on powerful back legs and carries its young in a pouch?
questions.explanation: Kangaroos use their strong back legs to hop and carry their young, called joeys, in a front pouch.

questions.prompt: Which slow moving Australian animal spends much of its day sleeping in eucalyptus trees and eating their leaves?
questions.explanation: Koalas sleep for many hours a day and eat mostly eucalyptus leaves, which are tough and low in nutrition.

questions.prompt: What is the name for the group of mammals, including kangaroos and koalas, that carry their young in a pouch?
questions.explanation: Marsupials are mammals whose young are born tiny and undeveloped, then finish growing in their mother's pouch.

questions.prompt: The platypus is unusual among mammals because it does what?
questions.explanation: The platypus is one of the very few mammals that lays eggs instead of giving birth to live young.

questions.prompt: Which spiky, egg laying Australian mammal is covered in sharp quills and eats ants and termites?
questions.explanation: The echidna, like the platypus, is a monotreme, one of the small group of mammals that lay eggs.

questions.prompt: What is the name for the small group of mammals, including the platypus and echidna, that lay eggs instead of giving birth to live young?
questions.explanation: Monotremes are a rare group of egg laying mammals, found only in Australia and New Guinea.

questions.prompt: Wombats are known for producing what unusually shaped droppings, thought to help stop them rolling away?
questions.explanation: Wombats produce roughly cube shaped droppings, which scientists think helps stop them rolling off logs and rocks used to mark territory.

questions.prompt: Kangaroos are well suited to Australia's dry conditions partly because they can do what with their water needs?
choices: Go long periods with very little water
Get all their water from the air
questions.explanation: Kangaroos are adapted to survive in dry, arid parts of Australia, needing far less water than many other large animals.

questions.prompt: Which flightless Australian bird, the second tallest bird in the world, has strong legs built for fast running across open country?
questions.explanation: The emu cannot fly, but its long, powerful legs let it run fast across the open plains it lives on.

questions.prompt: Many Australian eucalyptus trees are adapted to survive, and even benefit from, what natural event that regularly sweeps through dry Australian bush?
questions.explanation: Many eucalypts have thick bark, buried seed pods or roots that survive fire, and some species need the heat of a bushfire to release their seeds.

questions.prompt: What is the name of Australia's system of government, in which the country is led by a Prime Minister?
choices: A direct democracy with no parliament
questions.explanation: Australia is a parliamentary democracy, where the public elects members of parliament and the Prime Minister leads the government.

questions.prompt: In which city does Australia's federal Parliament meet?
questions.explanation: Australia's federal Parliament meets in Canberra, the city purpose built to be the national capital.

questions.prompt: Besides the federal government, Australia is divided into states and territories, each with their own what?
questions.explanation: Each Australian state and territory has its own parliament and government, alongside the federal government in Canberra.

questions.prompt: Unlike in many countries, voting in Australian federal elections is what for enrolled adult citizens?
questions.explanation: Australia requires enrolled adult citizens to vote in federal elections, one of a relatively small number of countries that does this.

questions.prompt: How many states make up Australia?
questions.explanation: Australia has six states, New South Wales, Victoria, Queensland, Western Australia, South Australia and Tasmania, plus two mainland territories.

questions.prompt: What are the two houses of Australia's federal Parliament called?
choices: The House of Representatives and the Senate
questions.explanation: Australia's federal Parliament has two chambers, the House of Representatives and the Senate.

questions.prompt: Who represents the King as Australia's head of state within the country, carrying out mostly ceremonial duties?
questions.explanation: The Governor-General represents the monarch in Australia and carries out mostly formal and ceremonial duties.

questions.prompt: In Australia's Senate, how many senators does each state get, regardless of the state's population?
questions.explanation: Each Australian state elects twelve senators, giving smaller states a stronger voice than their population alone would give them, while the two mainland territories elect fewer.

questions.prompt: Who usually becomes Australia's Prime Minister?
choices: The leader of the party or coalition with the most support in the House of Representatives
questions.explanation: The Prime Minister is normally the leader of whichever party or coalition can command a majority in the House of Representatives.

questions.prompt: Australia's system of voting for the House of Representatives asks voters to do what with the candidates, rather than just choosing one?
choices: Number every candidate in order of preference
Vote only for a party, not a person
Vote twice on two separate days
questions.explanation: Australia uses preferential voting, where voters number candidates in order of preference rather than picking just one.
